title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: reading the journey, measuring the time

questions.prompt: Read this club record, printed in the programme of a match played in 2026: "Club founded: 2004. First national title: 2009. In the first division without a break since: 2011. Present coach appointed: 2021." Which sentence about the club is right?

options.text: It has been playing in the first division for twenty-two years.
It has been playing in the first division since fifteen years.
It has had the same coach for seventeen years.
It has been playing in the first division for fifteen years.

questions.explanation: "It has been playing in the first division for fifteen years." is right: the record says the club has been up there without a break since 2011, and from 2011 to 2026 is fifteen years, which for measures as a length. "It has been playing in the first division for twenty-two years." counts from 2004, but 2004 is the year the club was founded, not the year it went up. "It has been playing in the first division since fifteen years." has the right number and the wrong word: since introduces the point where something starts, never a length. And "It has had the same coach for seventeen years." builds its figure on the first title, in 2009, whereas the present coach was appointed in 2021, five years before the match.

questions.prompt: Khaled, a coach from Gafsa, tells a school magazine: "I have been working with children for ten years now. I stopped playing in 2013, after a bad knee injury. Two years later I passed my coaching certificate, and the club offered me the junior team the following summer. I had joined that same club as a player back in 2004." In which order did these four events happen?

options.text: joining the club as a player → the knee injury → the coaching certificate → the junior team
the knee injury → joining the club as a player → the coaching certificate → the junior team
joining the club as a player → the coaching certificate → the knee injury → the junior team
the coaching certificate → joining the club as a player → the knee injury → the junior team

questions.explanation: "joining the club as a player → the knee injury → the coaching certificate → the junior team" is the true order, and Khaled gives it out of order on purpose. He joined as a player in 2004, the earliest date, which is why he tells it last and with a past perfect, I had joined. The injury stopped him in 2013. Two years later means 2015 for the certificate, and the following summer means 2016 for the junior team — ten years before the interview, exactly what for ten years now announces. "the knee injury → joining the club as a player → …" and "the coaching certificate → joining the club as a player → …" both take the sentence that comes last in the text for the event that comes first in time, although the past perfect says the opposite. And "joining the club as a player → the coaching certificate → the knee injury → …" puts the certificate before the injury, whereas two years later counts from 2013 and therefore lands after it.

questions.prompt: Complete this note with the right pair of words: "Emna booked her ___ from Tunis to Djerba — fifty minutes in the air — and once there, the silver ___ made in the island's workshops amazed her."

options.text: excursion / leaflet
voyage / jewellery
flight / jewellery
flight / galleries

questions.explanation: "flight / jewellery" is the right pair: fifty minutes in the air can only be a flight, a journey by plane, and the silver objects made in a workshop are jewellery. "voyage / jewellery" gets the second word right but calls the journey a voyage, which in English is a long journey by sea. "flight / galleries" gets the first word right and then puts galleries, the long rooms of a museum, in the place of the objects a workshop produces. And "excursion / leaflet" is wrong twice over: an excursion is a short outing made for pleasure, usually by a group, not a seat you book from Tunis to Djerba, and a leaflet is a printed sheet, not something made in silver.

questions.prompt: A swimming teacher in Bizerte says two things about herself. (1) "I have taught six hundred children to swim." (2) "I have been teaching at this pool since 2009." Which question does sentence (1) answer?

options.text: How long have you been teaching at this pool?
How many children have you taught to swim?
When did you teach your first swimming lesson?
Why did you decide to teach children to swim?

questions.explanation: "How many children have you taught to swim?" is the question sentence (1) answers: a present perfect simple with a number in it counts finished results, and six hundred children is exactly such a count. "How long have you been teaching at this pool?" asks for a length of time, and that is what sentence (2) answers, with its progressive form and its starting point since 2009. "When did you teach your first swimming lesson?" asks for a date, and no present perfect can give one — the answer would have to be a past simple, I taught my first lesson in 2009. And "Why did you decide to teach children to swim?" asks for a reason, which neither of the two sentences gives.

questions.prompt: In June 2026, Nizar says: "I have been working at the same garage in El Kef for six years." Which sentence gives exactly the same information?

options.text: I moved to El Kef six years ago and left the garage in 2020.
I have been working at that garage since 2020.
I have been working at that garage since six years.
I worked at that garage for six years and then I left.

questions.explanation: "I have been working at that garage since 2020." says the same thing in the other way: for measures the length, six years, and since names the point where that length begins — six years before June 2026, that point is 2020, and the tense keeps the job running today. "I have been working at that garage since six years." keeps the right idea but puts a length after since, which only accepts a point. "I moved to El Kef six years ago and left the garage in 2020." contradicts itself, since 2020 is the very year Nizar arrived, and it also ends the story that Nizar leaves open. And "I worked at that garage for six years and then I left." closes it with two past simples, whereas Nizar is still working there.

questions.prompt: Read this paragraph, then choose the best title for it. "Mouna had never left her governorate before. Last summer her school sent her to a camp in Bizerte for three weeks, with twenty students she had never met. She came home with forty new phone numbers, a taste for grilled fish and the firm idea that she would study languages. Her mother says she left a girl and came back a traveller."

options.text: A camp that lasted three weeks
How to choose your studies
Twenty students and a lot of fish
Three weeks that broadened a mind

questions.explanation: "Three weeks that broadened a mind" is the best title: the paragraph is not about the camp itself but about what three weeks away changed in Mouna — new friends, a new taste, a decision about her studies — and to broaden somebody's mind names exactly that change. "A camp that lasted three weeks" gives the frame of the story and leaves out everything that happened inside Mouna. "How to choose your studies" turns one single detail into a piece of advice, and the paragraph advises nobody. And "Twenty students and a lot of fish" collects two small details and drops the last sentence, which is where the point of the whole story lies.
